title: Apple and Meta Fight Canada Encryption Bill, Warn of Mass Surveillance
excerpt: Tech giants say Bill C-22 would force backdoors into WhatsApp and iMessage, putting billions of users at risk
body:
Apple and Meta are waging an unusually public campaign against Canada's Bill C-22, warning that the proposed Lawful Access Act would effectively force companies to build backdoors into encrypted messaging services — including WhatsApp and iMessage — opening the door to government surveillance on an unprecedented scale.

The bill, introduced by the Liberal government of Mark Carney, would require digital service providers to retain user metadata for one year and grant law enforcement and CSIS broad powers to demand access to private communications. Critically, the legislation's vague definition of encryption could compel companies to weaken end-to-end encryption, the security standard that ensures only sender and receiver can read a message.

**The Industry Pushback:** Apple argued in a formal submission that the bill would make Canadians *less safe*, not more, by creating systemic vulnerabilities that hackers and hostile states could exploit. Meta echoed the concern, warning of *sweeping powers* with *minimal safeguards.* The Electronic Frontier Foundation called the bill a repackaged version of last year's surveillance legislation that was shelved after public outcry.

The fight mirrors clashes playing out globally. The UK's Online Safety Act contains similar backdoor provisions that Apple has resisted, while EU proposals for client-side scanning of encrypted messages remain stalled. US lawmakers have joined the opposition, with a bipartisan group warning that Canadian backdoors could compromise American technology infrastructure and cross-border data flows.

**The Privacy Stakes:** For the 1.8 million people of Indian origin in Canada — the country's fastest-growing immigrant group — the implications are particularly acute. WhatsApp is the primary communication channel connecting families across the Indian diaspora, used for everything from family group chats to remittance coordination. A weakened encryption standard would expose these communications to potential government access without the robust judicial oversight that exists in the United States.

Michael Geist, Canada's leading digital policy expert, has highlighted that the bill's metadata retention requirements alone would create a detailed map of who communicates with whom — information that could be shared with foreign governments under existing intelligence-sharing agreements.

**What to Watch:** The bill heads to committee review, where tech companies and civil society groups are pushing for amendments requiring judicial warrants for all data access requests and removing provisions that could mandate encryption backdoors.
nri_angle: WhatsApp is the primary communication tool for 1.8 million Indian-origin Canadians and the broader diaspora; weakened encryption would expose family communications and remittance coordination to potential government surveillance.
author: Diaspora Desk
